title: USA Football Development Model: Player Progression Guide
author: USA Football (Football Development Model; ESPN-supported FDM Pilot Program)
source_note: USA Football Development Model (FDM) Player Progression Guide, 282 pages, full read via pymupdf. Domain football (catalog correct, American football). LTAD (long-term athlete development) framework spanning early childhood to high school; ESPN-supported FDM Pilot. Skill-decomposition ontology: Skill -> Progression Steps -> KPIs -> Drills. KPI = foundational action/movement identifying success/failure within a skill aspect (e.g. 'Cleats in the Grass' in passing Posture). Four stages: Stage 1 Discover&Play (no scoreboard/competition, fundamental movement run/jump/kick/throw/catch via play, 'everything is cross-training' Buddy Morris, transferable to any sport); Stage 2 Play&Develop; Stage 3 Develop&Achieve (sport-specific, compete, manage matchups, Rookie Tackle, tackle progression air->bags->controlled->full contact); Stage 4 Achieve&Advance (technical + tactical awareness, adolescence, decoupled physical/mental/emotional maturity, not high-school athletes). Matchup management = zone-of-proximal-development tradeoff (overmatched loses confidence; exploiting stalls improvement; equal competition optimal). Skill progressions: Passing (Pre-pass Grip/Base -> Posture Neutral -> Arm Mechanics Fluidity -> Finish Balance); Receiving (Feet -> Hands -> Vision/Locate -> Finish/Secure); Kicking (Prepare -> Contact Mechanics Eye-foot -> Power Leg-swing -> Finish Follow-through); Prep for Contact (global athleticism, fall/tumble/crawl safely); Blocking (remove helmet as contact tool, hands+hips, brace/pop step). Quantitative benchmarks: 7/10 hands-only catches on route, 7/10 leading partner, 15+ yd distance, Stage 4 20+ yd directional control. Preseason/postseason per-player written+online skill evaluation. Qualitative framework with proficiency benchmarks, no fitted statistical equations -> mostly no_equation_domain; hierarchy/progressions/matchup-tradeoff formalized as labeled structures. No sportsbook lines used as model inputs.

primitives.name: Football Development Model: long-term athlete development, developmentally appropriate
primitives.verbatim_quote: Based on long-term athlete development, the FDM is a framework helping parents, coaches and program leaders provide what players need to grow in a developmentally appropriate manner.
assumptions: The FDM is based on long-term athlete development (LTAD)
It spans early childhood into the high school years, providing developmentally appropriate growth
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a developmental framework, not a fitted law; it breaks down if training is imposed without regard to the athlete's developmental stage and maturity.

layer2.mapping: GSE LTAD stage-appropriate development IS this FDM framework: the engine models player development as long-term and stage-appropriate (training matched to developmental stage and maturity), the LTAD discipline that avoids premature specialization and age-inappropriate demands. GSI: long-term stage-appropriate development matched to maturity.
layer2.telemetry: FDM; LTAD; developmentally appropriate; early childhood to high school; 4 stages

primitives.name: Four developmental stages: Discover/Play, Play/Develop, Develop/Achieve, Achieve/Advance
primitives.verbatim_quote: This guide covers four stages of the Football Development Model.
assumptions: The four stages progress from free play to competitive technical/tactical football
Each stage has an overview, developmental checklist, skill progressions, KPIs, drills, and practice plans
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a staged developmental taxonomy, not an equation; it breaks down if stages are skipped or athletes are pushed ahead of their readiness.

layer2.mapping: GSE four-stage development taxonomy IS this FDM staging: the engine organizes player development into the four progressive stages (fundamental movement -> play -> sport-specific competition -> technical/tactical), the staged-readiness taxonomy gating skill introduction. GSI: staged developmental taxonomy gating skill introduction by readiness.

primitives.name: Skill decomposition: Skill -> Progression Steps -> KPIs -> Drills
primitives.verbatim_quote: Within each skill is a progression that provides steps to help players perform or coaches teach that skill.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Progression Step: an ordered sub-step of the skill [step]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.KPI: Key Performance Indicator within a step [indicator]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Drill: a training exercise targeting a KPI [exercise]

assumptions: Each skill contains an ordered progression of steps
Each progression step contains KPIs, and drills support each KPI; this gives coaches consistent language and keys
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a hierarchical skill-decomposition ontology, not a fitted equation; it breaks down if skills are taught as monoliths without decomposed steps and measurable KPIs.

layer2.mapping: GSE skill-decomposition ontology IS this Skill->Step->KPI->Drill hierarchy: the engine decomposes each football skill into ordered progression steps with measurable KPIs and supporting drills, the process-grade decomposition that gives consistent coaching keys and connects to execution-grade credit. GSI: hierarchical skill decomposition into ordered steps with measurable indicators.
layer2.telemetry: Skill -> Progression Steps -> KPIs -> Drills; consistent language; coaching keys

primitives.name: KPI: foundational action identifying success/failure within a skill aspect
primitives.verbatim_quote: KPIs are foundational actions or movements that identify reasons for success or failure within a specific aspect of the sport.
primitives.latex: \text{KPI}=\text{foundational action/movement}\Rightarrow \text{diagnoses success/failure of a skill aspect}
assumptions: A KPI is a foundational action or movement that identifies reasons for success or failure
Example: 'Cleats in the Grass' is a KPI within the passing Posture step; posture basics must be mastered to pass successfully
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a diagnostic-indicator definition, not a fitted equation; it breaks down if KPIs are outcome scores rather than foundational process actions.

layer2.mapping: GSE KPI process-diagnostic IS this definition: the engine uses KPIs as foundational process actions that diagnose success/failure of a skill aspect (e.g. 'Cleats in the Grass' for passing posture), the process-grade diagnostic that credits execution mechanics independent of outcome. GSI: foundational process-action indicators diagnosing skill-aspect success/failure.
layer2.telemetry: KPI foundational action; success/failure diagnosis; Cleats in the Grass; passing Posture

primitives.name: Stage 1: no scoreboard, no formal competition — activity and exposure
primitives.verbatim_quote: At this stage, there is no scoreboard nor is there formal competition. The focus is on activity and exposure.
assumptions: Stage 1 (Discover & Play) has no scoreboard or formal competition
The focus is activity and exposure; keep everyone moving, shrink games to their size, use appropriate-sized equipment
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a developmental-stage principle, not an equation; it breaks down if competitive scoring is imposed on early-childhood fundamental-movement play.

layer2.mapping: GSE early-stage exposure-over-outcome IS this Stage-1 principle: the engine recognizes that early development prioritizes activity/exposure and fundamental movement over competitive outcomes (no scoreboard), the exposure-first stage that builds the base before outcome pressure. GSI: early-stage exposure and fundamental movement before competitive outcome pressure.
layer2.telemetry: Stage 1; no scoreboard; no formal competition; activity/exposure; appropriate equipment

primitives.name: Everything is cross-training: fundamental skills transferable to any sport
primitives.verbatim_quote: You may use footballs and use football terminology in your drills, but what kids learn should be transferable to any sport or activity they join.
assumptions: Buddy Morris: 'At this age, everything is cross-training'
Early skills underpin everything learned later and should transfer to any sport, not just football
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a general-athleticism-before-specialization principle, not an equation; it breaks down if early training is narrowly sport-specific instead of transferable.

layer2.mapping: GSE transferable-fundamentals principle IS this cross-training stance: the engine values transferable fundamental movement skills (general athleticism) before narrow specialization, the broad-base-before-specialization discipline that builds robust athletic foundations. GSI: transferable fundamental skills before narrow specialization.
layer2.telemetry: everything cross-training; Buddy Morris; transferable to any sport; underpins later learning

primitives.name: Fundamental movement skills: run, jump, kick, throw, catch via play
primitives.verbatim_quote: Young children need the opportunity to develop basic movement skills such as running, jumping, kicking, throwing and catching in a fun setting built around informal play, exploration and positive reinforcement.
assumptions: Basic movement skills (running, jumping, kicking, throwing, catching) are developed through informal play
The setting is fun, exploratory, and positively reinforced; some children lack prerequisites and drills are adapted
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a fundamental-movement development principle, not an equation; it breaks down if technical drill replaces play-based fundamental movement at this stage.

layer2.mapping: GSE play-based fundamental movement IS this principle: the engine recognizes that basic movement literacy (run/jump/kick/throw/catch) is built through play and exploration with positive reinforcement, the movement-literacy foundation underlying all later technical skill. GSI: play-based fundamental movement literacy as the foundation for technical skill.
layer2.telemetry: run/jump/kick/throw/catch; informal play; exploration; positive reinforcement; adapt to prerequisites

primitives.name: Manage matchups: overmatched loses confidence, exploiting stalls development
primitives.verbatim_quote: A less skilled player who is overmatched consistently will lose confidence, which often can lead to giving up the sport, while a player with more refined skills who is allowed to exploit matchups may gain regular success but is not improving as rapidly as he or she would against someone of equal size, strength and talent.
primitives.latex: \text{development rate maximized at matched competition};\quad \text{overmatched}\rightarrow\text{confidence loss};\quad \text{exploiting}\rightarrow\text{slower improvement}
assumptions: Consistently overmatched players lose confidence and may quit
Players exploiting weaker matchups gain success but improve slower than against equal competition; manage matchups in practice and games
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a zone-of-proximal-development tradeoff, not a fitted equation; it breaks down if matchups are ignored (either chronic overmatch or chronic exploitation).

layer2.mapping: GSE matched-competition development IS this matchup-management tradeoff: the engine recognizes development is maximized at matched competition (overmatch erodes confidence, exploiting weaker opponents slows improvement), the zone-of-proximal-development discipline for practice and game matchmaking. GSI: development maximized at matched competition; balance confidence and challenge.
layer2.telemetry: overmatched -> confidence loss; exploiting -> slower improvement; equal competition optimal; manage matchups

primitives.name: Tackle progression: air -> bags -> controlled contact -> full contact
primitives.verbatim_quote: Young athletes just starting out in tackle football must show they possess the required skills against air and soft-sided bags before progressing to controlled contact and ultimately full contact.
assumptions: Tackle skills must be demonstrated against air and soft-sided bags first
Progression to controlled then full contact is gated on possessing the required skills; always cover basics before player-on-player contact
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a safety-gated skill progression, not an equation; it breaks down if full contact is introduced before the prerequisite skills are demonstrated.

layer2.mapping: GSE safety-gated contact progression IS this tackle progression: the engine models contact introduction as a skill-gated sequence (air -> bags -> controlled -> full contact), the safety-progression discipline that gates live contact on demonstrated prerequisite skill. GSI: safety-gated progression where live risk is unlocked only after prerequisite skill is shown.
layer2.telemetry: air -> bags -> controlled -> full contact; skill-gated; basics before player-on-player

primitives.name: Stage 4: technical skill plus dawning tactical awareness
primitives.verbatim_quote: Technical skill development and the dawning of tactical awareness mark athletes at this stage.
assumptions: Stage 4 (Achieve & Advance) combines technical skill with emerging tactical awareness
Players test more complex strategies in flag, 7-on-7, and full-field youth tackle; adolescence brings strength and speed
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a developmental-stage characterization, not an equation; it breaks down if tactical complexity is introduced before the technical base.

layer2.mapping: GSE technical-plus-tactical stage IS this Stage-4 characterization: the engine recognizes the stage where technical skill merges with tactical awareness (complex strategies), the technical-tactical integration stage preceding high-school competition. GSI: technical skill integrated with emerging tactical awareness.
layer2.telemetry: Stage 4; technical + tactical awareness; complex strategies; flag/7-on-7/youth tackle; adolescence

primitives.name: Maturity varies widely: physical, mental, emotional decoupled
primitives.verbatim_quote: The range of maturity levels are the most varied at this stage. Some athletes will have fully completed puberty while others may still be a year or two away.
assumptions: At Stage 4 maturity levels are most varied; some have completed puberty, others are years away
Physical, mental, and emotional maturity are decoupled: a physically developed teen may be emotionally immature, and vice versa
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a developmental-variability observation, not an equation; it breaks down if chronological age is used as a proxy for physical/mental/emotional readiness.

layer2.mapping: GSE decoupled-maturity model IS this variability observation: the engine treats physical, mental, and emotional maturity as decoupled dimensions (not chronological age), so readiness and matchups are assessed per-dimension, the biological-vs-chronological-age discipline. GSI: decoupled physical/mental/emotional maturity assessed per-dimension, not by chronological age.
layer2.telemetry: maturity most varied; puberty timing; physical vs mental/emotional decoupled; not high school athletes

primitives.name: These are not high school athletes — physically, mentally, emotionally
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, it's important to remember that these are not high school athletes. Not physically, mentally or emotionally.
assumptions: Stage 4 practices/rules resemble high school but the athletes are not high-school-ready
Coaches must not impose high-school physical/mental/emotional demands on pre-high-school athletes
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a developmental-caution principle, not an equation; it breaks down if high-school demands are imposed on younger athletes because the format resembles high school.

layer2.mapping: GSE format-not-readiness caution IS this principle: the engine recognizes that resembling a higher level's format does not mean the athletes are ready for its demands, the readiness-over-format discipline preventing age-inappropriate load. GSI: format resemblance does not imply readiness for higher-level demands.
layer2.telemetry: not high school athletes; physically/mentally/emotionally; format resembles but readiness differs

primitives.name: Passing progression: pre-pass position, posture, arm mechanics, finish
primitives.verbatim_quote: Creating a solid base from which to throw by having feet shoulder width apart, ball centered at chest, with a firm grip on the ball.
assumptions: Passing decomposes into pre-pass position (Grip, Base), Posture (Neutral Posture), Arm Mechanics (Fluidity), Finish (Balance)
Each step has KPIs: ankle/hip/shoulder pointed at target; single fluid motion; maintain balance on completion
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a skill-progression decomposition, not a fitted equation; it breaks down if throwing is taught as one motion without the decomposed posture/mechanics/finish steps.

layer2.mapping: GSE passing-mechanics decomposition IS this progression: the engine decomposes passing into pre-pass base/grip, neutral posture, fluid arm mechanics, and balanced finish with per-step KPIs, the mechanics-decomposition that grades throwing process step by step. GSI: decompose a motor skill into ordered mechanics steps with per-step indicators.
layer2.telemetry: pre-pass Grip/Base; Posture Neutral; Arm Mechanics Fluidity; Finish Balance; ankle/hip/shoulder to target

primitives.name: Receiving vision: track the ball into the hands, focus through distraction
primitives.verbatim_quote: Tracking the football through the air and into the hands. Learning to focus through distraction and with the body in various orientations.
assumptions: Receiving Vision is tracking the ball through the air into the hands
The KPI is Locate: judging depth and distance of a ball in flight, focusing through distraction and varied body orientations
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a perceptual-skill definition, not an equation; it breaks down if receiving is reduced to hands-only without the visual tracking/locate component.

layer2.mapping: GSE receiving-visual-tracking IS this Vision/Locate skill: the engine models receiving as visual ball-tracking (judging depth/distance, focusing through distraction) into the hands, the perceptual Locate component that precedes the physical catch. GSI: perceptual tracking/locate component preceding a physical interception skill.
layer2.telemetry: Vision; Locate; track ball into hands; depth/distance; focus through distraction

primitives.name: Prep for contact: global athleticism, fall/tumble/crawl safely
primitives.verbatim_quote: Not focused on sport-specific skills but on fundamental development of global athleticism
assumptions: Prep for Contact builds global athleticism, not sport-specific skills
KPIs: coordination, kinesthetic awareness, spatial awareness, balance, stability; ability to fall, tumble, crawl safely
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a general-athleticism preparation principle, not an equation; it breaks down if contact prep is sport-specific drill instead of global movement/fall safety.

layer2.mapping: GSE global-athleticism contact prep IS this principle: the engine models contact preparation as global athleticism and safe falling/tumbling/crawling (kinesthetic/spatial awareness, balance), the general-movement safety base before sport-specific contact. GSI: general athleticism and safe-fall movement base before specific contact skill.
layer2.telemetry: global athleticism; fall/tumble/crawl safely; kinesthetic/spatial awareness; balance/stability

primitives.name: Kicking power: multiple muscles and leg speed generate force at contact
primitives.verbatim_quote: Using multiple muscles and leg speed to generate strength behind the kick in order to achieve longer distance and/or height.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Power: force generated at contact via muscles + leg speed [N]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.leg-swing: the KPI for the Power step [motion]

assumptions: Kicking Power uses multiple muscles and leg speed to generate force for distance/height
The progression is Prepare (Body Position) -> Contact Mechanics (Eye-foot Coordination) -> Power (Leg-swing) -> Finish (Follow-through)
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a biomechanical principle (force from coordination + leg speed), not a fitted equation; it breaks down if power is reduced to leg strength alone without coordination and speed.

layer2.mapping: GSE kicking-force generation IS this Power principle: the engine models kick distance/height as force at contact from multi-muscle coordination and leg speed, the biomechanical force-generation chain (prepare -> contact -> power -> follow-through). GSI: force generation from coordinated multi-muscle action and segment speed.
layer2.telemetry: Power; multi-muscle + leg speed; force at contact; Prepare/Contact/Power/Finish; eye-foot coordination

primitives.name: Developmental benchmarks: 7-of-10 completion, distance thresholds
primitives.verbatim_quote: Catch 7 out of 10 accurately thrown balls with hands only while running a specified route
primitives.latex: \text{Stage 3 receiving benchmark}:\ \ge 7/10\ \text{hands-only catches on a specified route};\quad \text{passing}:\ 7/10\ \text{leading partner},\ 15+\ \text{yd for distance}
assumptions: Stage 3 checklist: catch 7/10 hands-only on a route; throw 7/10 leading a partner; throw 15+ yd for distance
Stage 4: 7/10 moving throws to stationary and moving targets; kick/punt 20+ yd with directional control
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: the 7/10 and yardage figures are developmental proficiency benchmarks, not fitted statistical laws; they break down if treated as precise population thresholds rather than stage checkpoints.

layer2.mapping: GSE stage proficiency benchmarks IS this checklist: the engine uses stage-specific proficiency benchmarks (7/10 completion, distance thresholds) as developmental checkpoints, the measurable readiness criteria gating progression between stages. GSI: stage-specific measurable proficiency benchmarks gating progression.
layer2.telemetry: 7/10 hands-only catches; 7/10 leading partner; 15+ yd; Stage 4 20+ yd directional; checkpoints

primitives.name: Preseason/postseason skill evaluation tracks individual progress
primitives.verbatim_quote: Long-term athlete development is at the core of the Football Development Model (FDM). This includes understanding player progress.
assumptions: Preseason and postseason assessments evaluate each individual player's development
Written + online per-player assessments gauge where players are in their progression and build plans to improve
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a longitudinal-assessment practice, not an equation; it breaks down if development is judged by a single snapshot rather than preseason/postseason progress.

layer2.mapping: GSE longitudinal player tracking IS this evaluation practice: the engine tracks individual player progress via preseason/postseason assessments (not a single snapshot), the longitudinal-development measurement that gauges progression and informs training plans. GSI: longitudinal pre/post assessment of individual progress, not single snapshots.
layer2.telemetry: preseason/postseason; per-player; written + online; gauge progression; build improvement plans

primitives.name: Blocking: remove helmet as contact tool, use hands with hips
primitives.verbatim_quote: Teach players to use the hands in conjunction with their hips
assumptions: Stage 4 blocking removes the helmet as a tool for contact
Players use hands in conjunction with hips; footwork and hand placement set up success; brace step and pop step establish position/power
primitives.breakdown_regime: no_equation_domain: a blocking technique/safety principle, not an equation; it breaks down if the helmet is used as the contact instrument rather than hands/hips.

layer2.mapping: GSE hands-hips blocking technique IS this principle: the engine models safe blocking as hands-in-conjunction-with-hips with helmet removed as a contact tool (footwork/hand placement, brace/pop steps), the technique-and-safety decomposition of blocking. GSI: technique decomposition emphasizing safe contact instruments (hands/hips, not helmet).
layer2.telemetry: remove helmet as contact tool; hands + hips; footwork/hand placement; brace step/pop step

reasoning_traces.think:
This inline cycle extracts the USA Football Development Model Player Progression Guide, a two-hundred-eighty-two-page youth-football development framework produced by USA Football with ESPN support for the FDM Pilot Program. The provenance is clean: the catalog domain football is correct and this is American football, the guide spans early childhood into the high school years, and it is organized around long-term athlete development. Eighteen primitives are extracted, each with a verified verbatim quote, a page anchor, assumptions, a breakdown regime, and a Layer-2 mapping with telemetry. The guide is a qualitative coaching and development framework with quantitative proficiency benchmarks but no fitted statistical equations, so most primitives are labeled no_equation_domain while the skill-decomposition hierarchy, the contact progression, and the matchup tradeoff are formalized as labeled structures, and no sportsbook line is used as a model input.

The retrocausal genealogy runs from the long-term athlete development (LTAD) literature and USA Football's Football Development Model into this progression guide, with the NFL strength-coaching tradition (Buddy Morris's 'at this age, everything is cross-training') informing the early-stage philosophy. The load-bearing object is the skill-decomposition ontology: each Skill contains an ordered set of Progression Steps, each step contains Key Performance Indicators, and drills support each KPI, giving coaches consistent language and diagnostic keys. A KPI is defined as a foundational action or movement that identifies reasons for success or failure within a specific aspect of the sport, exemplified by 'Cleats in the Grass' within the passing Posture step. The four stages (Discover and Play, Play and Develop, Develop and Achieve, Achieve and Advance) progress from no-scoreboard fundamental movement to technical skill merged with dawning tactical awareness.

The recursive theory of mind models the coach as a reasoner who must match training to the athlete's developmental stage and decoupled maturity, and the player as a developing agent whose confidence and improvement rate depend on matchup quality. The matchup-management principle is a zone-of-proximal-development tradeoff: a consistently overmatched player loses confidence and may quit, while a player exploiting weaker matchups gains success but improves more slowly than against equal size, strength, and talent, so development is maximized at matched competition. The tackle progression is safety-gated (air, then soft bags, then controlled contact, then full contact, each unlocked by demonstrated skill), and the maturity observation decouples physical, mental, and emotional readiness so chronological age is not a valid proxy. The passing, receiving, kicking, and blocking progressions decompose each motor skill into ordered mechanics steps with per-step KPIs.

The cross-layer veto adjudication places this player-development and skill-decomposition layer beside the rulebook constraint layer, the mental-conditioning layers, and the attribution and expected-points layers. The first veto is the skill-decomposition veto: skills are taught and graded as decomposed progression steps with measurable KPIs, not monoliths, connecting directly to the execution-grade process credit in the attribution layer (a KPI is a process grade). The second veto is the stage-appropriateness veto: training is matched to developmental stage and decoupled maturity, never imposing high-school demands because the format resembles high school. The third veto is the matched-competition veto: development is maximized at matched competition, balancing confidence against challenge, the zone-of-proximal-development discipline for practice and game matchmaking. The fourth veto is the safety-gated-contact veto: live contact is unlocked only after prerequisite skill is demonstrated against air and bags. The fifth veto is the longitudinal-measurement veto: player progress is tracked via preseason and postseason assessments, not a single snapshot, with quantitative proficiency benchmarks (seven-of-ten completion, distance thresholds) as stage checkpoints.

Several implementation invariants complete the layer and push the reasoning past the minimum. The early-stage philosophy prioritizes activity and exposure over competition (no scoreboard in Stage 1), builds fundamental movement literacy (run, jump, kick, throw, catch) through informal play and positive reinforcement, and insists the skills be transferable to any sport rather than narrowly football-specific. The passing progression runs pre-pass position (Grip, Base) to Posture (Neutral, ankle/hip/shoulder pointed at the target) to Arm Mechanics (Fluidity, a single fluid motion) to Finish (Balance); receiving runs Feet/Footwork to Hands to Vision (Locate, judging depth and distance through distraction) to Finish (Secure); kicking runs Prepare to Contact Mechanics (Eye-foot Coordination) to Power (Leg-swing, force from multi-muscle coordination and leg speed) to Finish (Follow-through). Prep for Contact builds global athleticism and safe falling/tumbling/crawling rather than sport-specific drill, and Stage 4 blocking removes the helmet as a contact tool in favor of hands working with hips. The developmental checklists also include a cognitive-affective dimension (taking turns, sharing, following simple directions, memorizing more complex plays at Stage 4), and each stage closes with sample practice plans and a shared drill glossary, so the framework couples physical skill with the social and cognitive maturity the game demands. The quantitative benchmarks (catch seven of ten hands-only on a route, throw seven of ten leading a partner, fifteen-plus yards for distance, twenty-plus yards with directional control at Stage 4) are developmental proficiency checkpoints, not population statistical laws. These invariants ground the engine's skill-decomposition process grading, stage-appropriate development, matched-competition matchmaking, safety-gated contact, and longitudinal player tracking, completing a sovereign player-development layer that connects KPI process grades to the attribution layer, all grounded in clean verbatim prose with honestly labeled formalizations.
